pinterest.title: Nigerian Wedding Traditions: Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani Customs, Family by Family
pinterest.description: Nigerian wedding traditions are not one set of customs. Yoruba families hold an introduction and an engagement ceremony led by two alaga hosts. Hausa-Fulani families marry with the nikah and welcome the bride at the kamu. In many Igbo families, the bride carries a cup of palm wine through the guests to find her groom. Our guide walks through each custom, then aso ebi and spraying, for Nigerian-Australian couples planning a wedding in Australia.

pinterest.title: Igba Nkwu: The Igbo Wine Carrying Ceremony at a Nigerian Wedding
pinterest.description: Igbo marriage moves in stages, and palm wine runs through all of them. At igba nkwu, the public ceremony, the bride's father pours her a cup of palm wine and asks her to show the gathering her husband. She walks through the guests in search of the groom, often hidden by his friends, and offers him the cup. Ask both families which stages they keep, and leave time on the run sheet for the search.

pinterest.title: Aso Ebi, Gele and Aso Oke: What Families Wear to a Nigerian Wedding
pinterest.description: At many Nigerian weddings, the families choose one fabric, the aso ebi, and each guest who takes part has an outfit made from it, so the room fills in blocks of colour. At many Yoruba weddings, the bride's gele is tied high and sculpted and the groom wears a fila. Aso oke is hand-woven in narrow strips, so order family cloth early, confirm lead times with the weaver and send guests the colours, fabric and ready-by date.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Nigerian wedding begins long before the wedding day. Two families meet, ask, answer, present gifts and settle a list, and only then does the public celebration arrive.

Customs differ between Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani families. At many Yoruba engagements, the groom and his friends lie prostrate before the bride's parents, and two alaga hosts keep the day moving with humour. Hausa-Fulani families marry with the nikah, and at the kamu the groom's family comes to collect the bride. In many Igbo families, the bride carries a cup of palm wine through the guests to find her groom, and the room waits for the moment she offers him the cup.

Some customs are shared. At many Nigerian weddings, family and close friends wear one aso ebi fabric, and guests dance up to the couple and spray notes on them while the band plays. Many couples also hold a church wedding or nikah on another day.

The best first step is a simple one: ask both families early which customs and stages they keep.

Our guide walks through each custom, then how Nigerian-Australian and mixed-heritage couples bring them to a wedding in Australia: ordering aso ebi from abroad, timing two ceremonies and planning a dance floor big enough for everyone.

newsletter.preview: Yoruba greetings, the Hausa-Fulani kamu, Igbo igba nkwu, aso ebi and spraying on the dance floor.
newsletter.blurb: A Nigerian wedding begins long before the wedding day, and its customs differ from family to family. Our new guide takes them in turn: the Yoruba introduction, prostrating greetings, gele and aso oke; the Hausa-Fulani nikah, kamu and lalle; and Igbo igba nkwu, when the bride carries palm wine through the guests to find her groom. Then aso ebi, spraying and the white wedding, with how Nigerian-Australian couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia.
